chapters.title: Chapter 4: Paying Tax Through the Year

lessons.title: Tax Audit, ITR-6 and Assessment: What Happens Before and After You File

body.text: Filing a return is not the end of the tax year. It is the moment your numbers enter a system that checks them, questions them, and occasionally rewrites them. Everything before the filing date is preparation, and everything after it is defence.

children.text: Most business owners picture tax compliance as one date in October. In reality a company passes through five stages: keeping books, getting them audited, getting them audited again for tax purposes, filing, and then living with whatever the department makes of it. This lesson walks the whole path.

Founders often assume their auditor does one job. A company actually faces two separate exercises, with different laws behind them. The statutory audit under the Companies Act applies to every company, however small, and produces the accounts your shareholders and lenders see. The tax audit under section 63 [old 44AB] applies only above certain thresholds, and produces a report for the tax department in Form No. 26.

body.caption: When a tax audit under section 63 [old 44AB] is required

cells: Business where cash receipts and cash payments are each within 5% of the total
Declaring profits below the presumptive rates in section 58 [old 44AD, 44ADA, 44AE]
Audit can be triggered regardless of turnover
Form No. 26, due one month before the return, so 30 September for a 31 October filer

body.text: The 5% cash test is worth engineering towards. A business that keeps cash receipts and cash payments each within 5% of the total gets a tax audit threshold of ₹10 crore instead of ₹1 crore. For a mid-sized trading business, moving suppliers and customers to bank transfers can remove an entire annual compliance exercise.

body.title: A company's compliance year, for tax year 2026-27

events.title: Tax year begins
events.description: Books open under section 62 [old 44AA]. Advance tax instalments run through the year as covered in Lesson 1.

events.title: Tax year ends
events.description: Close the books, settle statutory dues and unpaid micro and small supplier bills before this date to protect deductions.

events.title: Statutory audit under the Companies Act
events.description: Applies to every company regardless of size, and produces the audited financial statements.

events.title: Form No. 26 tax audit report
events.description: Filed by the chartered accountant and accepted by the company on the portal, one month before the return.

events.title: Return filed under section 263(1) [old 139(1)]
events.description: Companies file the corporate return, verified with a digital signature. Any balance paid now is self-assessment tax.

events.title: Processing and intimation under section 270 [old 143(1)]
events.description: The return is checked electronically for arithmetic, mismatches and obvious errors, and an intimation follows.

events.title: Scrutiny
events.description: A minority of returns are selected for detailed examination, conducted electronically through the portal.

children.text: What the Department Does With Your Return

cells: Automated check of arithmetic, internal inconsistencies and mismatches with reported TDS. Adjustments are proposed and you get thirty days to respond, then an intimation is issued showing a refund, a demand or nothing
A notice asking for evidence on specific items, answered through the portal. Ends in an assessment order that may accept or change your figures
Where a return is not filed or notices are ignored, the officer estimates income from available material, after giving a hearing
A later reopening where income is believed to have escaped assessment, subject to time limits and approvals
Reassessment provisions of the new Act
Correcting an apparent mistake, or appealing an order you disagree with
Rectification and appeal provisions of the new Act

body.text: Assessments are faceless. Notices arrive in your account on the income tax portal and by email, replies are uploaded, and there is no local officer to visit. The practical consequence is mundane but important: whoever holds the portal login must actually check it. Deadlines in these notices are short, and a missed reply is treated as no reply.

body.title: Quick Check: Who Needs a Tax Audit?
body.question: Four businesses close their year. Which one needs a tax audit under section 63 [old 44AB]?
options: A private limited company with turnover of ₹60 lakh, all through bank transfers
A trading firm with turnover of ₹4 crore, where 20% of receipts are in cash
A design consultancy with gross receipts of ₹42 lakh
A company with turnover of ₹8 crore, where cash receipts and payments are each under 5%
body.explanation: The trading firm crosses ₹1 crore and cannot use the ₹10 crore threshold, because its cash receipts exceed 5%. The ₹60 lakh company is below ₹1 crore. The consultancy is below the ₹50 lakh professional threshold. The ₹8 crore company qualifies for the ₹10 crore threshold because it stays within the 5% cash test, which is exactly the benefit of banking your receipts. Note that all four still need a statutory audit if they are companies, since that requirement has no size threshold.

children.text: Companies file the corporate return, known for years as ITR-6, under section 263 [old 139]. It must be verified with a digital signature, which means the director's signing token needs to be valid well before the due date. The same section also holds the belated return, allowed within nine months of the year end, and the revised return, allowed within twelve months.

body.title: Filing on time protects more than your reputation

columns.label: Filed by the due date
points: Business and capital losses can be carried forward under section 112 [old 72] and section 111 [old 74]
No late filing fee under section 428 [old 234F]
No interest under section 423 [old 234A] on unpaid tax
The return can still be revised within the allowed window

columns.label: Filed late
points: Losses of that year cannot be carried forward, though unabsorbed depreciation survives
Interest at 1% a month runs on tax still unpaid

body.title: Try It: The Cost of an Under-Reported Figure
body.prompt: During scrutiny, a company's taxable income is increased by ₹50,00,000. At an effective rate of 25.168%, the additional tax comes to ₹12,58,400. If this is treated as under-reporting rather than misreporting, what penalty applies under section 439 [old 270A]? Answer in ₹ lakh.
body.explanation: The penalty for under-reporting is 50% of the tax on the under-reported income, so ₹12,58,400 × 50% is ₹6,29,200, or about ₹6.29 lakh. That sits on top of the ₹12,58,400 of tax and the interest. Had the same addition been treated as misreporting, involving false entries or misrepresentation, the penalty would have been 200%, or ₹25,16,800.

body.title: Scenario: The Intimation Nobody Opened
body.scenario: A Coimbatore company filed its return on time in October, showing a refund of ₹3,40,000. In January an intimation arrived on the portal proposing an adjustment, because TDS of ₹4,10,000 claimed in the return did not match the credits appearing against the company's PAN. Nobody logged in. In March, a demand notice followed. The finance executive who handled the filing has since left, and her email was the registered contact.
body.prompt: What went wrong procedurally, and what should the company do now?
body.modelAnswer: The substantive issue is almost certainly a mismatch, not evasion. TDS credits appear against a PAN only when the deductor files its own return correctly, so a customer who deducted the company's TDS but filed late, quoted the wrong PAN or used the wrong tax year would produce exactly this gap. The procedural failure is what turned a fixable mismatch into a demand. Processing under section 270 [old 143(1)] proposes adjustments and allows thirty days to respond, and no response means the adjustment is made. Three things should happen now. First, regain control of the portal account and change the registered email and mobile to a role-based company address that survives staff changes. Second, download the tax credit statement, compare it line by line with the TDS claimed, and identify which deductors are missing or wrong. Then contact those customers and ask them to correct their TDS returns, since only the deductor can fix it. Third, respond to the demand through the portal, disagreeing where the credit is genuinely due and explaining the mismatch, and file a rectification once the corrected credits appear. If any part of the demand is genuinely payable, pay it promptly, because interest runs regardless of the reason for the delay. The broader lesson is that a filed return is not a closed file, and the portal inbox needs an owner.

body.title: Which law applies to an old year

children.text: Section 536 keeps earlier years under the old law. An assessment, notice, penalty or appeal relating to income earned up to 31 March 2026 continues under the Income-tax Act, 1961, with its original section numbers. A scrutiny notice quoting section 143(2) for such a year is correctly issued and should not be questioned on that ground.

This means a company can be dealing with both statutes at once for several years: the 2025 Act for current filings, the 1961 Act for an open assessment from 2024. Keep the two sets of files clearly labelled, and do not let a well-meaning adviser renumber references in old correspondence.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The Audit Report Deadline
body.textWithBlank: The tax audit report in Form No. 26 is due ___ month before the due date for filing the return.
body.explanation: One month. For a company filing by 31 October, the report is due by 30 September. Treating the two as a single October deadline is a common and expensive mistake, because the penalty for failing to get accounts audited is 0.5% of turnover, capped at ₹1,50,000.

body.label: The audit trail that decides everything
body.context: In scrutiny, a deduction is allowed because an invoice, a contract, a bank statement and a TDS challan exist. Explanations without documents rarely survive, and documents assembled after a notice arrives look exactly like documents assembled after a notice arrives.

body.title: Audit and Filing Readiness, Starting in April
steps: Keep the portal account under a role-based company email and mobile, not an individual employee's
Reconcile TDS claimed against the tax credit statement before filing, not after an intimation arrives
Confirm the director's digital signature is valid at least a month before the due date
Settle statutory dues, bonus and micro and small supplier bills before the year end or the filing date, as applicable
Give your auditor the fixed asset register, related party payments and TDS reconciliation early, since these produce most audit queries
Diarise both dates separately: the Form No. 26 report and the return
Keep contracts, invoices, bank proof and challans filed by vendor, so any single deduction can be evidenced in minutes
Check the portal inbox at least monthly, and treat every notice as having a thirty-day clock

cards.definition: The requirement to maintain books of account.
Tax audit, reported in Form No. 26, triggered mainly by turnover thresholds.
The Companies Act audit that every company must have, regardless of size, separate from the tax audit.
Processing of returns and regular assessment, including the intimation and scrutiny stages.
Best judgment assessment, used where returns are not filed or notices are ignored.
Penalty of 50% of tax on under-reported income, rising to 200% for misreporting.
The fee charged for filing a return after the due date.
Assessment conducted electronically through the portal, with no designated local officer to meet.

points: Every company faces a statutory audit under company law, and a tax audit under section 63 [old 44AB] only above the thresholds
Keeping cash receipts and payments each within 5% raises the tax audit threshold from ₹1 crore to ₹10 crore
Form No. 26 is due one month before the return, so 30 September against a 31 October filing date
Companies file under section 263 [old 139] with a digital signature, and filing on time is what preserves carried forward losses
After filing, returns are processed under section 270 [old 143(1)], with thirty days to answer proposed adjustments
Penalties run at 50% of tax for under-reporting and 200% for misreporting under section 439 [old 270A]
Assessments are faceless, so an unattended portal inbox turns small mismatches into demands
Years up to 31 March 2026 continue to be assessed under the 1961 Act, with its original section numbers

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax or legal advice. Section references reflect the Income-tax Act, 2025 as understood at the time of writing, with the corresponding 1961 Act section shown in brackets. Return form names and numbers for tax year 2026-27 are being updated for the new Act, and audit thresholds, deadlines and penalty provisions change. Confirm the current position on the income tax portal or with a qualified chartered accountant.
